researchResolution.reason: The source key marks C. RFC 3207 says STARTTLS negotiates TLS for SMTP, while RFC 6409 reserves 587 for submission; port 587 alone does not encrypt a session.

researchSources.title: RFC 3207: SMTP Service Extension for Secure SMTP over TLS
researchSources.supports: STARTTLS begins a TLS negotiation on SMTP; the protocol, not a port number alone, enables the TLS-protected session.

researchSources.title: RFC 6409: Message Submission for Mail
researchSources.supports: Port 587 is designated for message submission; the port designation does not by itself turn on TLS.

researchResolution.reason: Cisco's troubleshooting table lists a missing clock-rate command as a cause when a serial interface is up but line protocol is down in DCE mode. It separately describes no shutdown as the remedy for an administratively-down interface. That resolves the extracted conflict in favor of B; the extra A mark is incompatible with the stated interface state.

researchSources.title: Troubleshooting Serial Lines
researchSources.supports: For serial x up / line protocol down in DCE mode, a missing clockrate command is a possible cause; an administratively-down interface calls for no shutdown.

researchResolution.reason: RFC 1122 says off-network destinations are sent to a gateway; Ethernet address resolution maps the next-hop IP to its link-layer MAC address.

researchSources.title: RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts - Communication Layers
researchSources.supports: If the destination is not on a connected network, the host routes the datagram through a gateway.

researchSources.title: RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol
researchSources.supports: ARP maps a protocol address such as the next-hop IPv4 address to the Ethernet hardware address used for link-layer delivery.

researchSources.title: RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)
researchSources.supports: The Window field is a 16-bit field in the TCP header.

researchResolution.reason: RFC 5694 states that P2P peers both request and provide services, so option D is false. It describes decentralized control as a feature some authors associate with P2P but also notes that P2P systems may use centralized enrollment. The wording 'access control is decentralized' is therefore not universally established and does not exactly match the RFC's claim. Keep the question in review rather than treating B as certain.

researchSources.title: RFC 5694: Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Architecture
researchSources.relevantSection: Section 2, P2P definition; discussion of centralized enrollment and decentralized control
researchSources.supports: Peers both request and provide services; P2P systems can still have centralized enrollment, while decentralized control is described as an additional property in some definitions.

researchResolution.reason: Option C describes the weakness of SNMPv1/v2c community strings, which RFC 3410 characterizes as plain-text and weak authentication. SNMPv3 adds authentication and privacy; because the question does not name an SNMP version, the broad claim is not universally true.

researchSources.title: RFC 3410: Introduction and Applicability Statements for Internet-Standard Management Framework
researchSources.supports: RFC 3410 says SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c use plain-text community-string authentication, while SNMPv3 adds authentication and privacy capabilities.
